catalog_citation: Connell, Bruce A. 1991. Phonetic aspects of the Lower Cross languages and their implications for sound change. PhD thesis, University of Edinburgh, vol. 1. hdl:1842/19642; open copyhttps://core.ac.uk/download/429705670.pdf(scanned).
catalog_locator: Vol. 1, sec. 2.3.3.3, thesis pp.54-56 (fn.32 on p.55; fn.34 on p.56); tone statement sec. 2.2.2, p.47; Ekit in the 19-language list p.5.
catalog_quote: Ward (1933) attempted to account for the first kind of variation noted through reference to stress. She states that initial /t, k/ do not weaken intervocalically when verb root initial, and relates this to stress on the verb root ... Unfortunately, Ward's discussion of stress does not go any deeper than suggesting stress is related to verb stems, and in fact, it is difficult to find any true evidence for stress, at least in the sense proposed by Ward[32]. [fn. 32] This is not to assert that there is no stress at all in Efik or the other LC languages. There is likely some sort phrasal stress, and also the juncture between elements of compound words appears to be marked by stress, but these are clearly not what Ward was referring to. Faraclas (1984b) presents an analysis of Obolo incorporating phrasal stress. [fn. 34, p.56] ... as the foot is a notion usually associated with stress phenomena, it is by no means clear how it would apply in a non-stress language. [p.47] The system that exists throughout LC is one of two basic tones, High (H = ') and Low (L = v), which may combine on a given syllable (with restricted and varying distribution) to give Falling (H+L = "), and less frequently, Rising (L+H = ") tones. ... In addition to these two basic tones, there is also a phonologically significant Downstep (Ds = !) ... Lower Cross languages can therefore be characterized as being two-toned, terraced level languages.
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ekit, like all Lower Cross languages, is a two-tone (H, L) terraced-level language with contrastive downstep (p.47: 'Lower Cross languages can therefore be characterized as being two-toned, terraced level languages'). Connell finds no real evidence for word-level (verb-root) stress of the kind Ward (1933) proposed for Efik and calls Lower Cross 'a non-stress language'; he allows only for some kind of phrasal stress and stress marking the juncture inside compounds. No word-stress position rule is given for Ekit or any Lower Cross language.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the only hedge is that 'some sort [of] phrasal stress' and compound-juncture stress may exist (fn. 32). Connell 1994 (JWAL 24(1), p.12) repeats that tone 'appear[s] to be further complicated through interaction with phrasal stress, but except for Faraclas (1984b) for Obolo, no investigation in this area has been done.'
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the Lower Cross group as a whole (Efik discussed directly, 'the other LC languages' by extension); any stress is phrasal or compound-juncture, not word-level. Ekit data in the thesis are Connell's own taped wordlists (560+ items) and sentence lists, tone-marked, no stress marking (Appendix A / Blench-site Unicode wordlist held).
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding statement is a group-level one for the Lower Cross languages (Efik-centred, explicitly extended to 'the other LC languages'); Ekit is one of the 19 languages in Connell's study, with Connell's own field data (thesis p.5, pp.13-14), and Connell 1994 p.5 notes Ekit has two dialects (unnamed). No Ekit-specific prosodic description exists. Blench's Atlas (2011, entry 107) lists Connell 1991 as the sole source for Ekit. Wikipedia mislabels the language's glottocode as ekit1245; the correct one is ekit1246. Some older classifications treat Ekit/Eket as part of the Ibibio-Efik cluster (Ethnologue: 'Also use Efik').

sources.note: p.5: Ekit 200,000 speakers, two dialects. Sec. 3.3 p.10: 'in all languages of the group, there are two tones, high (H) and low (L), and contrastive downstep'; Ekit (with Efai, Efik) retains the older no-spreading tone situation; p.11 Ekit has contrastive vowel length. Sec. 5 p.12: tonal systems 'further complicated through interaction with phrasal stress, but except for Faraclas (1984b) for Obolo, no investigation in this area has been done.' No word-stress statement.
